_comment: Grade 5 grammar practice for the standalone app: one 'Let us talk' round and one Fluency Practice question per grammar item, authored by hand from each item's own rule text. Grade 5's ruleAndExamples set wrong forms beside right ones and explain in sentences of their own, so they cannot be parsed into examples the way Grades 2-4 are; this file replaces that parse for Grade 5. Wrong options are the unit's own taught mistakes, or real English that does not answer the situation - never a second correct answer. Read by ../grade-1-app/build-lessons.py when app.config.json names it (grammarPractice). Never written into the unit JSON: the Grade 5 shell course is not to change.
origin: AI-authored 2026-09-11 from each Grade 5 grammar item's own rule text, pending curriculum review

talk.ask: Your team has just won the football match, and you want to say how you feel about them. What do you say?
talk.say: I am proud of my team.
wrong: I am proud my team.
I am proud for my team.
talk.why: Proud takes of: proud of my team. Take the preposition away and the sentence breaks.

fluency.ask: Which sentence is complete and correct?
fluency.answer: The villagers were grateful for the hidden stream.
wrong: The villagers were grateful the hidden stream.
The villagers were grateful of the hidden stream.
The villagers grateful for the hidden stream.
fluency.why: Grateful takes for when you name the thing, and the sentence still needs its verb, were.

talk.ask: Your friend asks which school subject you enjoy. What do you say?
talk.say: I am interested in history.
wrong: I am interested on history.
I am interested at history.
talk.why: Interested is one of the fifteen pairs: interested in.

fluency.ask: Which word completes the sentence? She is good ___ running.
wrong: in
on
for
fluency.why: Good takes at: good at running.

talk.ask: You broke your sister's pencil by accident. What do you say to her?
talk.say: I am sorry about the pencil.
wrong: I am sorry with the pencil.
I am sorry to the pencil.
talk.why: Sorry about is for something you did yourself.

fluency.ask: Which sentence uses the right preposition after grateful?
fluency.answer: I am grateful to my teacher for her help.
wrong: I am grateful for my teacher for her help.
I am grateful with my teacher for her help.
I am grateful at my teacher for her help.
fluency.why: Grateful to the person, grateful for the thing they gave.

talk.ask: You want to describe the elder from the fable in a few words. What do you say?
talk.say: The noble elder spoke wisely.
wrong: The noble of elder spoke wisely.
The noble for elder spoke wisely.
talk.why: An adjective standing right in front of its noun needs no preposition.

fluency.ask: Which sentence is correct?
fluency.answer: A misty morning greeted the village.
wrong: A misty of morning greeted the village.
A misty about morning greeted the village.
A misty with morning greeted the village.
fluency.why: Misty sits in front of morning, so no preposition is needed.

talk.ask: Your little brother does not like the night. What do you say about him?
talk.say: He is afraid of the dark.
wrong: He is afraid from the dark.
He is afraid the dark.
talk.why: Afraid takes of. From is the wrong preposition, and leaving it out breaks the sentence.

fluency.ask: Which sentence has been fixed correctly?
wrong: She is good in maths.
She is good on maths.
She is good maths.
fluency.why: Good at maths - the unit's own repair of the wrong preposition.

talk.ask: Someone asks which sport you like most. What do you say?
talk.say: I am keen on football.
wrong: I am keen of football.
I am keen at football.
talk.why: Keen takes on: keen on football.

fluency.ask: Which word completes the sentence? He is responsible ___ the garden.
wrong: of
about
with
fluency.why: Responsible takes for: responsible for the garden.

talk.ask: You want to tell visitors that all people may come to the fair. What do you say?
talk.say: Everyone is welcome at the fair.
wrong: Nobody is welcome at the fair.
Everyone are welcome at the fair.
talk.why: Everyone means all people, and it takes a singular verb, is.

fluency.ask: Which word completes the sentence? ___ left a bag in the hall, but we do not know who.
wrong: Everyone
Nothing
Several
fluency.why: Someone means an unknown person.

talk.ask: Your group has checked the rocket model twice. What do you tell your teacher?
talk.say: Everything has been checked twice.
wrong: Everything have been checked twice.
Everything were checked twice.
talk.why: Everything is singular, so it takes has.

fluency.ask: Which sentence is correct?
fluency.answer: Nobody knows where the book went.
wrong: Nobody know where the book went.
Nobody are knowing where the book went.
Nobody have known where the book went.
fluency.why: Nobody is singular: nobody knows.

talk.ask: You were out, and you want to check whether a person phoned you. What do you ask?
talk.say: Did anyone call me?
wrong: Did anyone called me?
Anyone did call me?
talk.why: Questions use anyone, and after did the verb stays in its base form: call.

fluency.ask: Which sentence is correct?
fluency.answer: I cannot find anything in my bag.
wrong: I cannot find nothing in my bag.
I cannot find nobody in my bag.
I not can find anything in my bag.
fluency.why: After not, use anything. Not with nothing makes a double negative.

talk.ask: Everyone in your class needs a packed lunch for the trip. What do you tell them?
talk.say: Everyone should bring their own lunch.
wrong: Everyone should bring they're own lunch.
Everyone should bring there own lunch.
talk.why: Their is the belonging word. They're means they are, and there is a place.

fluency.ask: Which sentence uses its apostrophes correctly for a friendly blog?
fluency.answer: We've finished the model, and you'll love it.
wrong: Weve finished the model, and youll love it.
We'have finished the model, and you'll love it.
We've finished the model, and yo'ull love it.
fluency.why: The apostrophe stands where the missing letters were: we have becomes we've, you will becomes you'll.

talk.ask: Your friend asks when and where the astronauts landed. What do you say?
talk.say: In 1969, the astronauts landed on the Moon.
wrong: The astronauts landed.
In 1969 the astronauts, landed on the Moon.
talk.why: In 1969 tells when and on the Moon tells where; an opening adverbial takes a comma after it.

fluency.ask: Which sentence tells HOW the crew checked the equipment?
fluency.answer: The crew checked the equipment carefully before the launch.
wrong: The crew checked the equipment.
The crew checked the equipment at the space centre.
The crew checked the equipment last night.
fluency.why: Carefully tells how. At the space centre tells where, and last night tells when.

talk.ask: You are reading your repaired blog aloud to the class. Which sentence do you read?
talk.say: Somebody has left their notebook on the desk.
wrong: Somebody have left they're notebook on the desk.
Somebody has left they're notebook on the desk.
talk.why: Somebody takes has, and the belonging word is their.

fluency.ask: Which sentence has no mistakes?
wrong: Nobody don't know the winner yet.
Nobody doesn't know the winner yet.
Nobody know the winner yet.
fluency.why: Nobody is already negative and singular: nobody knows.

talk.ask: You are comparing two poems, a haiku and a ballad. What do you say about their length?
talk.say: A haiku is shorter than a ballad.
wrong: A haiku is the shortest than a ballad.
A haiku is more shorter than a ballad.
talk.why: Two things take the comparative with than: shorter than.

fluency.ask: Which sentence compares THREE OR MORE things?
fluency.answer: She is the best poet in our class.
wrong: She is a better poet than me.
The river poem is wilder than the haiku.
A haiku is shorter than a ballad.
fluency.why: The best poet in our class ranks one against the whole group - a superlative.

talk.ask: You felt better after your presentation than before it. What do you say?
talk.say: I felt happier after the presentation.
wrong: I felt happyer after the presentation.
I felt more happier after the presentation.
talk.why: Happy ends in -y: change the y to i and add -er.

fluency.ask: Which words complete the sentence? Our rules are ___ than the old ones.
wrong: inclusiver
more inclusiver
most inclusive
fluency.why: Inclusive has three syllables, so it takes more and stays as it is.

talk.ask: Your friend asks which test question was the least difficult. What do you say?
talk.say: This was the easiest question on the test.
wrong: This was the easyest question on the test.
This was easiest question on the test.
talk.why: Easy becomes the easiest: y to i, add -est, and put the in front.

fluency.ask: Which sentence is correct?
fluency.answer: That is the most beautiful poem I have ever read.
wrong: That is the beautifulest poem I have ever read.
That is most beautiful poem I have ever read.
That is the more beautiful poem I have ever read.
fluency.why: A long adjective takes the most, with the in front.

talk.ask: You want to say that your friend writes better than you do. What do you say?
talk.say: She is a better writer than I am.
wrong: She is a gooder writer than I am.
She is a more good writer than I am.
talk.why: Good is irregular: good, better, best.

fluency.ask: Which word completes the sentence? That was the ___ storm in years.
wrong: baddest
most bad
worse
fluency.why: Bad is irregular: bad, worse, worst. The superlative is worst.

talk.ask: You are comparing your height with your sister's. What do you say?
talk.say: I am taller than my sister.
wrong: I am more taller than my sister.
I am taller my sister.
talk.why: Never use -er and more together, and include than when you name both people.

fluency.ask: Which sentence has been fixed correctly?
wrong: He is fastest runner.
He is the most fastest runner.
He is the faster runner of all.
fluency.why: A superlative takes the, and one-syllable fast takes -est on its own.

talk.ask: In your reflection you compare the two seasons. What do you write?
talk.say: The rainy season is more colourful than the dry season.
wrong: The rainy season is colourfuller than the dry season.
The rainy season is the more colourful than the dry season.
talk.why: Colourful is a long adjective, so it takes more ... than.

fluency.ask: Which sentence uses its comparison correctly?
fluency.answer: The grass grows greener than an emerald.
wrong: The grass grows more greener than an emerald.
The grass grows greenest than an emerald.
The grass grows greener an emerald.
fluency.why: Green is short: greener than.

talk.ask: Your friend asks which girl saved the village. What do you say?
talk.say: The girl who found the spring saved the village.
wrong: The girl which found the spring saved the village.
The girl, who found the spring, saved the village.
talk.why: Who is for people, and a defining clause takes no commas.

fluency.ask: Which word completes the sentence? The spring ___ lay beneath the dunes was hidden for centuries.
wrong: who
whose
what
fluency.why: Which is for things; who is for people.

talk.ask: You want to say which teacher was so animated. What do you say?
talk.say: The teacher who told us the legend was very animated.
wrong: The teacher was very animated who told us the legend.
The teacher which told us the legend was very animated.
talk.why: The clause goes straight after its noun, and teacher takes who.

fluency.ask: Which sentence puts the clause straight after its noun?
fluency.answer: The explorer who made the discovery shared the map.
wrong: The explorer shared the map who made the discovery.
Who made the discovery the explorer shared the map.
The explorer shared who made the discovery the map.
fluency.why: Park the clause immediately after the noun it defines: the explorer who made the discovery.

talk.ask: The dog barked all night. It belongs to your neighbour. Join the two ideas. What do you say?
talk.say: The dog that barked all night belongs to my neighbour.
wrong: The dog that it barked all night belongs to my neighbour.
The dog that barked all night it belongs to my neighbour.
talk.why: That replaces it, so it must not appear again.

fluency.ask: Which sentence folds these two into one? The map was old. It showed the route to the dunes.
fluency.answer: The map that showed the route to the dunes was old.
wrong: The map that it showed the route to the dunes was old.
The map was old that showed the route to the dunes.
The map, that showed the route to the dunes, was old.
fluency.why: The second sentence becomes the clause, straight after the map, with no extra it and no commas.

talk.ask: You point out your brother in the crowd. What do you say?
talk.say: The boy who is wearing a red hat is my brother.
wrong: The boy, who is wearing a red hat, is my brother.
The boy, who is wearing a red hat is my brother.
talk.why: The clause tells us which boy, so it takes no commas.

fluency.ask: Which sentence follows the no-comma rule for defining clauses?
fluency.answer: The girl who scored the goal celebrated with her team.
wrong: The girl, who scored the goal, celebrated with her team.
The girl who scored the goal, celebrated with her team.
The girl, who scored the goal celebrated with her team.
fluency.why: Defining means no commas.

talk.ask: You tell a friend about a book you borrowed. What do you say?
talk.say: The book which I borrowed was interesting.
wrong: The book who I borrowed was interesting.
The book which I borrowed it was interesting.
talk.why: A book is a thing, so which, and the clause needs no extra it.

fluency.ask: Which sentence has been repaired correctly?
fluency.answer: The cat which caught the mouse was fast.
wrong: The cat which it caught the mouse was fast.
The cat who it caught the mouse was fast.
Caught the mouse the cat was fast.
fluency.why: The doubled subject it is removed, and the clause sits after the cat.

talk.ask: Your teacher asks what your group has arranged for next week. What do you say?
talk.say: We are presenting the report next week.
wrong: We presenting the report next week.
We are present the report next week.
talk.why: An arranged plan takes am, is or are with the -ing form: we are presenting.

fluency.ask: Which sentence uses the verb that naturally goes with its noun?
fluency.answer: We made a discovery at the well.
wrong: We did a discovery at the well.
We took a discovery at the well.
We reached a discovery at the well.
fluency.why: The collocation is make a discovery.

talk.ask: Your friend has written hopefull at the end of a sentence. What do you tell them?
talk.say: Hopeful has one l, because -ful as a suffix only has one.
wrong: Hopeful has two ls, just like the word full.
Hopeful should end in -fully when it comes last.
talk.why: The word full has two ls, but the suffix -ful has one.

fluency.ask: Which spelling is correct? She thanked her teacher ___.
wrong: gratefuly
gratefullly
greatfully
fluency.why: Add -ly to grateful and the l doubles: gratefully.

talk.ask: Your friend asks what always happens when you heat ice. What do you say?
talk.say: If you heat ice, it melts.
wrong: If you heat ice, it will melted.
If you heated ice, it melts.
talk.why: A result that always follows uses the present simple twice.

fluency.ask: Which sentence states a result that happens EVERY time?
fluency.answer: If the temperature drops below zero, water freezes.
wrong: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay inside.
If you try this experiment, you will see something surprising.
If we do not water the garden today, the flowers will wilt.
fluency.why: Two present simple verbs and no will: a fact, the zero conditional.

talk.ask: You explain what happens when red and blue paint are mixed. What do you say?
talk.say: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
wrong: If you mix red and blue you get, purple.
If you will mix red and blue, you get purple.
talk.why: If + present simple, then a comma, then the present simple result.

fluency.ask: Which sentence uses the comma correctly?
fluency.answer: If you press the button, the light turns on.
wrong: If you press the button the light, turns on.
If, you press the button the light turns on.
If you press, the button the light turns on.
fluency.why: When the if-clause comes first, the comma goes straight after it.

talk.ask: You are about to drop an egg on the kitchen floor right now. What does your mum warn you?
talk.say: If you drop that egg, it will make a mess on the floor.
wrong: If you dropped that egg, it will make a mess on the floor.
If you will drop that egg, it will make a mess on the floor.
talk.why: One future event takes the first conditional: present simple, then will.

fluency.ask: Which sentence is a FIRST conditional, about one future event?
fluency.answer: If you heat the water, it will be ready for tea.
wrong: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils.
If plants do not get sunlight, they die.
If you drop an egg, it breaks.
fluency.why: It will be ready is one occasion, so will. The others are facts that happen every time.

talk.ask: You are telling a friend the first step of the rice recipe. What do you say?
talk.say: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear.
wrong: You rinsing the rice until the water runs clear.
Rinsed the rice until the water runs clear.
talk.why: An instruction opens with the imperative: the base verb and no subject.

fluency.ask: Which instruction is written as an imperative?
wrong: You stir the onion.
The onion is stirred.
Stirring the onion.
fluency.why: An imperative never carries a subject: stir the onion.

talk.ask: You tell your friend what to do while the rice soaks. What do you say?
talk.say: While the rice soaks, chop the onion.
wrong: While the rice soaks, chopped the onion.
While, the rice soaks chop the onion.
talk.why: While joins the two actions, the comma closes the while-clause, and the step is an imperative.

fluency.ask: Which sentence closes a set of instructions?
fluency.answer: Finally, lift the lid and separate the grains with a fork.
wrong: First, rinse the rice.
Next, stir in the crushed garlic.
Before you start, wash your hands.
fluency.why: Finally is a closer. First and before you start open a sequence; next carries the middle.

talk.ask: Your friend asks where the pot goes. What do you say?
talk.say: Place the pot on the stove.
wrong: Place the pot between the stove.
Place the pot under the stove.
talk.why: On means resting on a surface. Between needs two things, and under puts the pot beneath the stove.

fluency.ask: Which word completes the instruction? Leave a gap ___ the plate and the bowl.
wrong: beside
above
under
fluency.why: Between means in the middle of two things.

talk.ask: Your partner spells noticable and asks if it looks right. What do you say?
talk.say: It is noticeable, because the e stays to keep the c soft.
wrong: It is right, because you always drop the e before -able.
It is noticible, because the ending is -ible.
talk.why: Notice keeps its e before -able, an exception to the drop-the-e rule.

fluency.ask: Which word breaks the rule 'i before e, except after c'?
wrong: piece
believe
receive
fluency.why: Weird has ei with no c before it, so it breaks the rule; the other three follow it.

talk.ask: The rule was unfair. The students protested. Join the two ideas smoothly. What do you say?
talk.say: The rule was unfair, so the students protested.
wrong: The rule was unfair, but the students protested.
The rule was unfair so, the students protested.
talk.why: So gives the result. But would mark a contrast that is not there.

fluency.ask: Which word is a connective adverb that links one whole sentence to the next?
wrong: and
because
but
fluency.why: However opens a new sentence. And and but join inside a sentence, and because hangs a smaller idea on a bigger one.

talk.ask: Your friend asks whether the task was hard. It was long, but you still finished on time. What do you say?
talk.say: The task was long, yet we finished on time.
wrong: The task was long, so we finished on time.
The task was long, or we finished on time.
talk.why: Yet shows a surprising contrast.

fluency.ask: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
fluency.answer: Amal read and shared the letters.
wrong: Amal read, and shared the letters.
The trial began and, the room grew quiet.
The trial began, and, the room grew quiet.
fluency.why: One subject with two actions takes no comma; a comma goes before the conjunction only when it joins two complete sentences.

talk.ask: Your teacher asks why the students protested. What do you say?
talk.say: They protested because the rule was unfair.
wrong: They protested because, the rule was unfair.
Because the rule was unfair.
talk.why: With the main clause first, no comma. A because-clause on its own is unfinished.

fluency.ask: Which sentence uses the comma correctly?
fluency.answer: Although it rained, they kept working.
wrong: Although it rained they, kept working.
Although, it rained they kept working.
Although it rained. They kept working.
fluency.why: When the subordinate clause comes first, a comma closes it.

talk.ask: The evidence was clear. You want to give the result in a new sentence. What do you say next?
talk.say: Therefore, the rule was changed.
wrong: However, the rule was changed.
Therefore the rule, was changed.
talk.why: Therefore shows a result and takes a comma straight after it. However would mark a contrast.

fluency.ask: Which words complete the second sentence? Some readers love adventure. ___, others prefer realistic fiction.
wrong: Therefore
As a result
Furthermore
fluency.why: On the other hand introduces the opposite view.

talk.ask: You are starting your retelling of the story. What do you say first?
talk.say: First, the children took their seats in the courthouse.
wrong: Finally, the children took their seats in the courthouse.
In the end, the children took their seats in the courthouse.
talk.why: First opens the sequence. Finally and in the end close it.

fluency.ask: Which opener shows two events happening at the same time?
wrong: Finally
Firstly
Eventually
fluency.why: Meanwhile shows two events together.

talk.ask: You are writing a formal report and want to add one more finding. What do you write?
talk.say: Furthermore, they found more letters.
wrong: And they found more letters.
Furthermore they found, more letters.
talk.why: Formal writing swaps an opening And for a connective adverb such as furthermore, followed by a comma.

fluency.ask: Which one is a complete sentence?
fluency.answer: Because it rained, they worked inside.
wrong: Because it rained.
Because it rained, inside.
They worked inside because.
fluency.why: A because-clause needs a main clause to hang on.

talk.ask: Your friend asks for your opinion of the mural. What do you say?
talk.say: I think that the mural is beautiful.
wrong: The mural was painted on a wall in the old hall.
The mural is on a wall.
talk.why: An opinion reports your view. The other two are facts that can be checked.

fluency.ask: Which sentence is a FACT?
fluency.answer: Ghana is a country in West Africa.
wrong: I believe that Ghana holds the best festivals.
Ghana has the most exciting music.
In my opinion, Ghana is beautiful.
fluency.why: A fact can be checked. Best, most exciting and beautiful are judgement words.

talk.ask: In a formal talk, you want to give your view of the mural. What do you say?
talk.say: In my opinion, the mural is a symbol of hope.
wrong: In my opinion the mural, is a symbol of hope.
In my opinion that the mural is a symbol of hope.
talk.why: In my opinion opens formally and takes a comma straight after it.

fluency.ask: Which sentence adds a reason to an opinion?
fluency.answer: I think that the mural shows pluralism because it holds many different people.
wrong: I think that the mural shows pluralism.
The mural holds many different people.
The mural shows pluralism, I think.
fluency.why: Because adds the reason.

talk.ask: In a debate, you want to share a view you would defend hardest. What do you say?
talk.say: I believe that every child deserves a good education.
wrong: It seems to me that every child might deserve a good education.
I feel cold that every child deserves a good education.
talk.why: I believe signals a deep conviction. It seems to me is the weakest, and I feel cold is a physical feeling.

fluency.ask: Which sentence describes a PHYSICAL feeling?
wrong: I feel that the characters are brave.
I believe that kindness matters.
I think that the story is exciting.
fluency.why: I feel cold is a feeling in the body, so it drops the word that.

talk.ask: Your classmate says the ending was sad, and you see it differently. What do you say politely?
talk.say: I see your point, but I think that the ending was hopeful.
wrong: I disagree.
You are wrong about the ending.
talk.why: Name their idea, give your own view, then your reason. I disagree alone sounds abrupt.

fluency.ask: Which reply names the other idea, gives a view and adds a reason?
fluency.answer: I respect your opinion, but I disagree because the ending was hopeful.
wrong: I disagree.
That is a good point.
No, the ending was hopeful.
fluency.why: All three steps are there: respect, view, and a reason with because.

talk.ask: Your friend asks whether the story is good. Give your opinion with a reason. What do you say?
talk.say: I think that the story is good because it teaches us about memory.
wrong: I think that the story is good.
The story is good, I think that.
talk.why: An opinion is stronger with its reason: because it teaches us about memory.

fluency.ask: Which of these is a fact, so it should NOT be written as an opinion?
fluency.answer: The sun rises in the east.
wrong: Sunrises are the loveliest part of the day.
The story is exciting.
The ending was surprising.
fluency.why: The sun rising in the east can be checked. I think that would dress a fact as an opinion.

talk.ask: You are Omar, retelling the market day in your own words. Which sentence keeps your viewpoint?
talk.say: I wiped my counter and waited for the boats.
wrong: He wiped his counter and waited for the boats.
I wiped his counter and waited for the boats.
talk.why: A first-person retelling stays with I and my from start to finish.

fluency.ask: Which sentence punctuates the direct speech correctly?
wrong: “The fish are here”, shouted Omar.
“The fish are here.” shouted Omar.
The fish are here, “shouted Omar.”
fluency.why: The comma goes before the closing quotation mark, and only the spoken words sit inside the marks.

talk.ask: A classmate asks what current means in 'the current youth history programme'. What do you say?
talk.say: Here current means happening now.
wrong: Here current means a flow of water in a river.
Here current means a flow of electricity.
talk.why: A homonym has several meanings, and the sentence picks one: a programme can be happening now.

fluency.ask: In 'We bought juice at the school fair', what does fair mean?
wrong: just and equal
light in colour
not heavy
fluency.why: You buy juice at an event, so fair here is the school event.

talk.ask: Your friend asks if you know the museum. You went there once. What do you say?
talk.say: I have visited the museum.
wrong: I have visit the museum.
I has visited the museum.
talk.why: Have or has plus the past participle; I takes have.

fluency.ask: Which sentence is correct?
wrong: I have seen him yesterday.
I have saw him yesterday.
I seen him yesterday.
fluency.why: Yesterday is a named past time, so the past simple, not the present perfect.

talk.ask: Someone asks how long you have lived in your town. You moved there in 2020. What do you say?
talk.say: I have lived here since 2020.
wrong: I have lived here for 2020.
I live here since 2020.
talk.why: Since names the point where it started, and it sits inside the present perfect.

fluency.ask: Which word completes the sentence? We have studied English ___ three months.
wrong: since
from
during
fluency.why: Three months is a length of time, so for.

talk.ask: Your friend asks how the ceremony was. It was amazing. What do you say?
talk.say: The ceremony was truly magnificent.
wrong: The ceremony was very more magnificent.
The ceremony was magnificently truly.
talk.why: The adverb of degree sits in front of the adjective it strengthens.

fluency.ask: Which sentence puts the adverb of degree in the right place?
wrong: She is talented extremely.
Extremely she is talented.
She extremely is talented.
fluency.why: Extremely goes straight in front of talented.

talk.ask: You describe a vase you saw in the museum. What do you say?
talk.say: It is a lovely small blue ceramic vase.
wrong: It is a blue small lovely ceramic vase.
It is a ceramic lovely blue small vase.
talk.why: Opinion, size, colour, material: lovely small blue ceramic.

fluency.ask: Which phrase has its adjectives in the right order?
wrong: a wooden round old table
a round wooden old table
an old wooden round table
fluency.why: Age, shape, material: old round wooden.

talk.ask: You want your reader to hear how loud and wild the wind was. What do you say?
talk.say: The wind howled like a frightened wolf.
wrong: The wind howled loudly.
The wind howled like a quiet whisper.
talk.why: A simile works when the two things share a quality: both make a loud, wild sound.

fluency.ask: Which sentence is a simile?
fluency.answer: The night was as dark as a cave.
wrong: The night was very dark.
The cave was dark at night.
The night was darker than the day.
fluency.why: As ... as compares two unlike things that share a quality.

talk.ask: In your persuasive speech, you want to make your strongest claim about the school garden. What do you say?
talk.say: Every school must protect its garden.
wrong: Every school might protect its garden.
Every school could protect its garden.
talk.why: Must is the strongest modal. Could and might only suggest a possibility.

fluency.ask: Which modal verb shows only a possibility?
wrong: must
should
will
fluency.why: Could suggests a possibility; must and should press much harder.

talk.ask: Your friend asks how to spell the word for a doctor in the poster. What do you say?
talk.say: It is physician, and the f sound is spelled ph.
wrong: It is fisician, spelled the way it sounds.
It is phisician, with an i after the ph.
talk.why: Physician, physics and philosophy all spell the f sound with ph.

fluency.ask: Which word has the same ou sound as pour?
wrong: hour
touch
soup
fluency.why: Pour and four are both said with the or sound; hour, touch and soup say ou three other ways.

talk.ask: Your friend asks what you call the mark a foot leaves in the mud. What do you say?
talk.say: It is a footprint.
wrong: It is a printfoot.
It is a footing.
talk.why: Foot + print: the mark that a foot leaves behind.

fluency.ask: Which compound noun means a book that guides you?
wrong: textbook
clipboard
footprint
fluency.why: Guide + book = guidebook.

talk.ask: You are waiting for the bus with a friend. Where do you say you are?
talk.say: We are at the bus stop.
wrong: We are at the busstop.
We are at the stop bus.
talk.why: Bus stop is an open compound: two words that name one thing.

fluency.ask: Which compound noun is written in the HYPHENATED form?
wrong: textbook
bus stop
woodland
fluency.why: Close-up links its two words with a hyphen.

talk.ask: The sun is coming up, and your friend asks what that is called. What do you say?
talk.say: It is the sunrise.
wrong: It is the risesun.
It is the sunrising.
talk.why: Noun + verb: sun + rise = sunrise.

fluency.ask: Which compound noun is built from a VERB + a NOUN?
wrong: wildlife
sunrise
textbook
fluency.why: Break + fast. Wildlife is adjective + noun, sunrise is noun + verb, textbook is noun + noun.

talk.ask: You are retelling the forest mission. Which sentence do you say?
talk.say: Amal looked around at the woodland paths.
wrong: Amal looked around at the wood land paths.
Amal looked around at the landwood paths.
talk.why: Woodland is a closed compound: wood + land, written as one word.

fluency.ask: In 'TALIA enters downstage right', which compound noun is built from a preposition + a noun?
wrong: first-aid
clipboard
footpath
fluency.why: Down + stage: a preposition and a noun.

talk.ask: You tell your teacher which book you read at home. What do you say?
talk.say: I read my textbook.
wrong: I read my text book.
I read my text-book.
talk.why: Textbook is a closed compound, so it is not split or hyphenated.

fluency.ask: Which plural is correct?
wrong: mother-in-laws
mothers-in-laws
mother-ins-law
fluency.why: A hyphenated compound adds -s to its main noun: mothers.

talk.ask: Your friend asks what you call a coat that keeps the rain off. What do you say?
talk.say: It is a raincoat.
wrong: It is a coatrain.
It is a rain's coat.
talk.why: Rain + coat = raincoat.

fluency.ask: What does the compound noun waterfall mean?
fluency.answer: water that falls from a high place
wrong: a fall that happens near water
a place where water is stored
a coat that keeps water off
fluency.why: Build the meaning from the parts: water that falls.

talk.ask: Your class is ready to begin the showcase. What do you tell your teacher?
talk.say: Everyone is ready.
wrong: Everyone are ready.
Everyone ready.
talk.why: Everyone takes a singular verb, and a sentence needs its verb.

fluency.ask: Which sentence is correct?
fluency.answer: I am proud of my board.
wrong: I am proud for my board.
I am proud my board.
I proud of my board.
fluency.why: Proud of, and the sentence needs its verb, am.

talk.ask: Your teacher asks about your draft. You finished it this morning. What do you say?
talk.say: I have finished my draft.
wrong: I have finish my draft.
I finishing my draft.
talk.why: The present perfect: have plus the past participle, finished.

fluency.ask: Which sentence talks about an arranged future plan?
wrong: We have presented already.
If you rehearse, you feel calmer.
We presented last Friday.
fluency.why: Are presenting with a future time is an arranged plan.

talk.ask: Someone in the audience says the mural matters, and you agree. What do you say?
talk.say: I agree, because it saved a piece of history.
wrong: I agree.
No, it does not.
talk.why: Agree and add your reason, so the speaker learns something from your reply.

fluency.ask: Which one is a correct yes/no question?
fluency.answer: Did the project change your mind?
wrong: Did the project changed your mind?
The project did change your mind?
Why did the project change your mind?
fluency.why: Did + subject + base verb. Why makes it a wh- question.

talk.ask: You describe the box on your display table. What do you say?
talk.say: It is a small old wooden box.
wrong: It is a wooden old small box.
It is an old small wooden box.
talk.why: Size, age, material: small old wooden.

fluency.ask: Which phrase uses a superlative correctly?
wrong: the most clearest page
the clearer page of all
the more clearest page
fluency.why: A short adjective takes -est, with the in front, and never most as well.

talk.ask: Your teacher asks why you revised your work. What do you say?
talk.say: We revised because the feedback helped.
wrong: We revised because, the feedback helped.
Because the feedback helped.
talk.why: With the main clause first, no comma; and a because-clause cannot stand alone.

fluency.ask: Which one uses a relative clause correctly?
fluency.answer: This is the page that I liked best.
wrong: This is the page that I liked it best.
This is the page, that I liked best.
This is the page who I liked best.
fluency.why: That replaces it, takes no commas, and page is a thing, not a person.

talk.ask: You read your final sentence aloud to check it. Which version do you read?
talk.say: Nobody knows how hard we worked.
wrong: Nobody know how hard we worked.
Nobody don't know how hard we worked.
talk.why: Nobody is singular and already negative: nobody knows.

fluency.ask: Which sentence has no mistakes?
wrong: Everyone have finished their project.
Everyone has finished they're project.
Everyone has finish their project.
fluency.why: Everyone has, their for belonging, and the past participle finished.
